title: Abstinences
hookLine: right speech, action and livelihood as moments of mind, not just rules

cards: Dinner with friends, and someone brings up a person who isn't there. A remark is ready on the tongue: a joke that would land, and sting. The mouth is already open, the laugh around the table half imagined.
Then it closes again, and someone passes the bread. Nothing was said. And yet the Abhidhamma says something did happen in that moment, something specific enough to have its own name.

teach.b: The manual calls it virati, abstinence, and it names three. Right speech: turning away from lies, harsh words, divisive talk and idle chatter. Right action: turning away from killing, stealing and sexual misconduct.
Right livelihood: turning away from earning a living in harmful ways. In the suttas these are part of the eightfold path, a way of life.
In the Abhidhamma they become something smaller and sharper: a mental factor that arises in the very moment the mind turns away from a wrong it could have done. Not a rule on a wall. A moment.
The commentaries tell a story to show it.
A young man named Cakkana had a mother who was very sick, and a doctor said fresh hare's meat would cure her. He went to the field and caught a hare.
Then, holding it, he thought: it isn't right to take one life to save another, even my mother's. He let it go.
Tradition says he came home, solemnly declared that he had never knowingly harmed a living being, and his mother recovered.
The commentators use the story for one kind of abstinence: refraining when the chance arrives, with no vow made beforehand.
They name two more: refraining because of precepts one has taken, and a last kind that comes with awakening, when the urge is uprooted for good.
The Dhammapada gathers the three doors in one verse, in Max Müller's words: "The wise who control their body, who control their tongue, the wise who control their mind, are indeed well controlled."
A precept kept for years is made of moments. Each time the hand doesn't take and the tongue doesn't cut, a fresh moment of virati arises. Restraint isn't only something a person has.

how: Some lay Buddhists formally take the five precepts at a temple or before a monk, and Abhidhamma students learn the three abstinences of right speech, right action and right livelihood as mental factors that arise when a wrong is refrained from.

o: moments when the mind turns away from a wrong
days when temples close their doors to visitors
a monk's promise never to speak again

games.q: a moment of restraint: tap the pairs.
p: turning from lies and harsh words

s: in the Abhidhamma, abstinence is a rule written down
it's a mental factor: the moment the mind turns away from a wrong.
in the commentary story, Cakkana kills the hare to save his mother
he lets it go. tradition says his mother recovered.
the commentaries name a kind of abstinence that needs no vow beforehand
Cakkana's kind: refraining when the chance arrives.

games.q: you're Cakkana. your mother is very sick, a doctor says hare's meat will cure her, and you're holding a hare. what do you do?
o: take it home: it's for your mother.
keep it and ask the doctor again.
games.why: in the commentary story he lets it go, unwilling to take one life to save another. tradition says his mother recovered.

practice: If you'd like, bring to mind one small thing you'd rather not do, a sharp reply, a bit of gossip, a small fib to smooth things over, and rehearse the moment it would come, and the turning away.
Not a vow, just the turning, once, here, so it's familiar when it arrives. Notice what turning away is like: a small pause, a hand that stays still, a breath.

wordCard.voice: Abstinences. Virati: the moment the mind turns away from a wrong in speech, action or livelihood. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali virati: abstinence, the mind turning away from a wrong in the moment.

carryVoice: Your line: a moment of restraint. Like Cakkana in the field, opening his hands. Until tomorrow.
